title: First aid & Stop the Bleed
note: Covers bleeding control, CPR and AED use, choking, and common medical, injury, and environmental emergencies as described by the 2025 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC, the 2024 AHA and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid, the American College of Surgeons Stop the Bleed program, CDC, and NHS guidance as of 2026-11-04. Refresh yearly and after any new AHA, Red Cross, or Stop the Bleed guideline release. This is study material and does not replace hands-on training: take an in-person Stop the Bleed course and a CPR/AED course and renew them on schedule.

concepts.n: Scene safety, checking the person, and the recovery position
concepts.s: Make sure the scene is safe for you, check whether the person responds and breathes normally, and use the recovery position only for an unresponsive person who is breathing normally and has no suspected spine injury.

x.b:
The 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross first aid guidelines open with a general rule: give care within your skill and knowledge, get further medical help as needed, and stay mindful of your own safety.

  1. Look before you go in. Traffic, fire, electricity, water, an active threat, or a hazardous substance can turn one patient into two.
  2. Check responsiveness. AHA Heartsaver teaching for 2025: tap the shoulders and shout for an adult or child; tap the foot and shout for an infant.
  3. Check breathing. Scan the chest for at least 5 and no more than 10 seconds. No breathing, or only gasping, means start CPR.
  4. Shout for help and get the phone and AED moving (see the CPR concepts).

The 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines say it is reasonable to place a person with decreased alertness from a nontraumatic cause, who is breathing normally, in a side-lying recovery position. Anyone who needs CPR or rescue breaths goes flat on the back instead.

  • Roll the person onto their side so the mouth points downward and fluids can drain. Bend the top leg to stop them rolling forward.
  • The guidelines note the recovery position has been associated with delayed recognition of respiratory arrest. Keep watching the breathing and roll them back and start CPR if it stops or becomes gasping.
  • For a suspected neck, back, hip, or pelvic injury in a person who is responsive and breathing normally, the guidelines say to leave them in the position found unless the area is unsafe.

The AHA adult BLS guideline describes agonal breathing as slow, irregular gasping that does not move enough air. It is common early in cardiac arrest, and lay rescuers often mistake it for a sign the person is still breathing. Treat gasping as no breathing and start compressions.

Trap: Moving a responsive trauma patient "to make them comfortable." If they are breathing normally and the area is safe, leave them as found.
Trap: Spending long on a pulse check. AHA guidance tells lay rescuers to rely on unresponsiveness plus absent or abnormal breathing, without a pulse check.

cards.q: How long should a lay rescuer spend checking breathing before deciding to start CPR?
cards.a: At least 5 and no more than 10 seconds, per AHA Heartsaver 2025 teaching.

cards.q: A collapsed adult is making occasional slow gasps. Breathing or not?
cards.a: Not breathing normally. Agonal gasps are a sign of cardiac arrest, so start CPR.

cards.q: Who belongs in the recovery position?
cards.a: A person with decreased alertness from a nontraumatic cause who is breathing normally.

cards.q: What is the main risk of the recovery position that the 2024 guidelines flag?
cards.a: It can delay recognition that breathing has stopped, so you must keep monitoring.

cards.q: Responsive, breathing normally, suspected neck or back injury: what positioning do the 2024 guidelines advise?
cards.a: Leave the person in the position found unless the area is unsafe.

concepts.n: Calling 911 and what to tell the dispatcher
concepts.s: Call 911 early, give the exact location first, stay on the line, and follow the dispatcher's instructions because they can coach CPR and other care while help is on the way.

x.b:
1. Location first. Street address, building type, nearest cross street or landmark, and the specific floor, room, or apartment. Minneapolis 911 lists location details first for this reason.
  2. What happened. "Adult collapsed, not breathing." "Gunshot wound to the thigh, heavy bleeding."
  3. Answer the call taker's questions and do not hang up until they end the call. Help can be dispatched while you are still talking.
  4. If calling is unsafe, text 911 where text-to-911 is available.

x.t: Speakerphone and the dispatcher as coach
x.b: The 2025 AHA guidelines tell telecommunicators to coach lay rescuers through Hands-Only CPR for adults and conventional CPR with breaths for children. Put the phone on speaker so your hands stay free. Stop the Bleed teaching (the "A" in its ABCs is Alert) also starts with calling 911.

• Point at one specific person: "You in the blue jacket, call 911 and come back." A crowd addressed generally tends to assume someone else did it.
  • Send a second person for the AED and the bleeding control kit.
  • Send someone to the building entrance to guide responders in.

Trap: Driving a person with chest pain or stroke signs to the hospital yourself. AHA advice for heart attack symptoms is to call 911 and not drive yourself; EMS can start treatment and alert the hospital.
Trap: Hanging up as soon as you have given the address. Stay on the line.

cards.q: What is the first piece of information to give a 911 call taker?
cards.a: Your exact location, including floor, room, or apartment and a cross street or landmark.

cards.q: Why put the phone on speaker during a cardiac arrest?
cards.a: So your hands stay free for compressions while the dispatcher coaches you.

cards.q: When should you hang up on 911?
cards.a: Only when the call taker ends the call.

cards.q: What should you do if it is not safe to speak to 911?
cards.a: Text 911 where text-to-911 is available.

concepts.n: Good Samaritan laws and consent (US, general)
concepts.s: US Good Samaritan laws generally protect bystanders who give reasonable emergency help in good faith, though details vary by state and none of this is legal advice.

x.b: Good Samaritan statutes exist across the US and vary by state. EBSCO's legal overview describes the core idea as immunity from lawsuits for accidental injury when a bystander helps in an emergency. It also notes protection generally does not extend to conduct that is malicious or reckless, and some state laws are written mainly for trained personnel acting within their training.

A separate category protects people who call 911 during a drug overdose. EBSCO reports that New Mexico passed the first such law in 2007 and that, with Kansas (2024) and Wyoming (2025), all 50 states and DC had some version by mid-2025. These laws generally shield the caller and the person overdosing from certain possession charges. Coverage differs by state. The 2025 AHA guidelines also call for legal protection of lay rescuers who give naloxone in good faith.

• Ask a responsive adult before helping: "I know first aid. Can I help you?" A refusal from a competent adult should be respected; call 911 anyway if the situation is serious.
  • For an unresponsive person, standard first aid teaching treats consent as implied.
  • For a child, ask a parent or guardian if one is present.
  • Once you start, stay until someone with equal or higher training takes over, or until it is unsafe to continue.

Synthesis: The legal risk of acting reasonably in an emergency is low compared with the cost of doing nothing. The conduct that loses protection is gross deviation: doing things far outside your training, acting recklessly, or abandoning the person. Look up your own state's statute if you want specifics.
Trap: Assuming you need a certification card to be protected. Lay rescuers are the main audience for these laws; training helps your skill, and the statutes vary on whether it matters legally.

cards.q: What do Good Samaritan laws generally protect?
cards.a: Bystanders who give reasonable emergency help in good faith, from liability for accidental harm. Details vary by state.

cards.q: What conduct generally falls outside Good Samaritan protection?
cards.a: Malicious or reckless conduct, per EBSCO's overview.

cards.q: What do overdose Good Samaritan laws protect?
cards.a: The person who calls 911 and the person overdosing from certain drug possession charges; coverage varies by state.

cards.q: How is consent handled for an unresponsive adult?
cards.a: It is treated as implied, so you can give care.

concepts.n: Recognizing life-threatening bleeding (Stop the Bleed ABCs)
concepts.s: The American College of Surgeons Stop the Bleed course teaches Alert (call 911), find the Bleeding, and Compress, and it defines life-threatening bleeding by what you see: spurting, soaking, or continuous pooling blood.

x.b:
1. A: Alert. Call 911, or tell a specific person to call. Make sure the scene is safe and wear gloves if you have them.
  2. B: Bleeding. Expose the wound by opening or cutting away clothing and find where the blood is coming from.
  3. C: Compress. Direct pressure, wound packing, or a tourniquet, depending on location and severity.

The ACS Stop the Bleed lay presentation lists:

  • Blood spurting from a wound.
  • Blood soaking through clothing or bandages.
  • Continuous, large-volume bleeding, or blood pooling on the ground.

It also warns that bleeding can come from more than one site and that clothing can hide it. The ACS material calls bleeding the leading cause of preventable death after injury, and the Los Angeles Fire Department's Stop the Bleed page adds that severe bleeding can kill in as little as 5 minutes.

ACS teaching groups wounds by location because it decides the tool: arms and legs (tourniquet territory), the neck, armpits, and groin (junctional areas, packing and pressure), and the torso (pressure only; get to a trauma center fast).

Trap: Looking at the person's face instead of the wound. Expose the body and look, including the back and under heavy clothing.
Trap: Waiting for EMS to arrive before acting. Bleeding can kill before any ambulance can arrive, which is why the program exists.

cards.q: What do the Stop the Bleed ABCs stand for?
cards.a: Alert (call 911), Bleeding (find it), Compress (pressure, packing, or tourniquet).

cards.q: Name three signs of life-threatening bleeding taught by Stop the Bleed.
cards.a: Spurting blood, blood soaking through clothing or bandages, and continuous or pooling blood.

cards.q: Why must you expose the wound?
cards.a: Clothing hides the source and the amount of bleeding, and there may be more than one wound.

cards.q: According to ACS, what is the leading cause of preventable death after injury?
cards.a: Bleeding.

concepts.s: Firm, continuous pressure aimed at the bleeding source controls most bleeding, and deep or large wounds need gauze packed into the cavity with pressure held on top.

x.b:
• Put gauze or any clean cloth directly on the bleeding point, then push hard with both hands, using your body weight. ACS teaching says to use only enough material to cover the wound so your force stays concentrated.
  • If pressure stops the bleeding, keep holding until help arrives.
  • The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines put this first: direct pressure, followed by a tourniquet or wound packing where the wound location allows.

ACS teaches that surface pressure does not work for large or deep wounds, because the bleeding vessel sits below the surface.

  1. Expose the wound and find the bleeding source.
  2. Push gauze (hemostatic gauze if available, plain gauze or clean cloth if not) into the wound, directly onto the bleeding point.
  3. Keep feeding and packing until the wound is full and no more fits.
  4. Hold firm pressure on top until help arrives.

Hemostatic dressings carry an agent that speeds clotting and appear in many public-access kits. They work only with packing and pressure; the agent does not replace your force. If none is available, plain gauze or cloth packed the same way is the standard fallback in Stop the Bleed teaching.

Trap: Lifting the dressing to check whether it worked. That breaks the clot that is forming. If blood soaks through, add more material on top and press harder, or pack.
Trap: Spreading a thick wad of bandages over a wide area. Thick, wide padding spreads your force. Aim small and press hard.
Trap: Pressure points and limb elevation as primary bleeding control. Current Stop the Bleed and AHA/Red Cross sequences are direct pressure, packing, and tourniquet; pressure points are absent from them.

cards.q: What is the first step to control external bleeding?
cards.a: Firm direct pressure on the bleeding source with both hands.

cards.q: Why does surface pressure fail in a deep wound?
cards.a: The bleeding vessel is below the surface, so the gauze must be packed down onto it.

cards.q: When is wound packing finished?
cards.a: When no more gauze fits; then hold firm pressure on top.

cards.q: Blood soaks through the dressing. Remove it or add more?
cards.a: Add more on top and press harder; removing it disrupts the clot.

cards.q: Does hemostatic gauze work without pressure?
cards.a: No. It must be packed and held with firm pressure.

concepts.s: For life-threatening limb bleeding, place a commercial tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound and not over a joint, tighten until the bleeding stops, note the time, and leave it on.

x.b:
1. Place the band on the limb 2 to 3 inches above the wound, between the wound and the heart. It can go over clothing (ACS).
  2. Do not place it over a joint (elbow or knee). If 2 to 3 inches lands on a joint, go above the joint.
  3. Pull the strap as tight as you can and fasten it.
  4. Twist the windlass rod until the bleeding stops. ACS teaching warns it will be painful; tell the person.
  5. Lock the windlass in its clip and secure it with the strap.
  6. Note the time it went on, on the tourniquet strap or by telling responders.
ACS teaching: if the first tourniquet is as tight as it can go and the bleeding continues, place a second one just above the first (closer to the torso) and tighten it the same way.

• ACS material states that no amputations were caused by tourniquets left in place for less than 2 hours, and that losing a limb is preferable to dying from bleeding.
  • The adult tourniquet works on all but very young children, per ACS. For infants and very small children, direct pressure usually works and packing follows the adult technique.
  • ACS says training tourniquets should not be used on real patients, because repeated training use can cause failure.
  • You can put one on yourself.

Stop the Bleed teaches 2 to 3 inches above the wound. Tactical medicine also teaches "high and tight" (as high on the limb as possible) when the wound cannot be found quickly, under threat, or for untrained responders, according to a North American Rescue explainer that cites the tactical care committees.

Synthesis: For a civilian who can see the wound, follow the course rule. If you cannot find the source on a limb that is clearly bleeding to death, high on the limb is a reasonable fallback, and the second-tourniquet rule still applies.

Trap: Tightening only until the bleeding slows. A partly tightened tourniquet can block the veins and leave the arteries flowing, which can make bleeding worse. Tighten until the bleeding stops.
Trap: Loosening it to "give the limb a break." ACS: leave it on. Removal is a hospital decision.

cards.q: Where does Stop the Bleed teach placing a tourniquet?
cards.a: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, between the wound and the heart, and not over a joint.

cards.q: When have you tightened the tourniquet enough?
cards.a: When the bleeding stops.

cards.q: The first tourniquet is maximally tight and bleeding continues. Next step?
cards.a: Apply a second tourniquet just above the first and tighten it.

cards.q: What should you record after applying a tourniquet?
cards.a: The time it was applied, and tell responders.

cards.q: What does ACS teaching say about tourniquets left on under 2 hours?
cards.a: No amputations were caused by tourniquets in place for less than 2 hours.

concepts.s: Improvised tourniquets usually fail to stop arterial bleeding, so carry a commercial windlass tourniquet and use pressure and packing as the fallback.

x.b: The ACS Stop the Bleed lay presentation states that improvised (homemade) tourniquets are much less effective than commercial ones such as the C-A-T, and are hard to make and apply well without extensive practice. Its photos show recommended commercial models including the C-A-T, SOF-TT, SAM-XT, TX3, TMT, and RMT.

Synthesis: A belt or a narrow cord cannot be pulled tight enough by hand to squeeze an artery shut, and without a rigid windlass there is no mechanical advantage to finish the job. A partial squeeze blocks the veins first, which can make bleeding worse. A rigid stick windlass on a wide cloth band is the improvised design most likely to work, and it is still a fallback.

If no tourniquet is available, use what the course teaches works with no equipment: hard direct pressure, then packing.

Trap: "Tourniquets are a last resort and always cost the limb." ACS teaching: tourniquets are safe with recommended models, and no amputations resulted from tourniquets in place under 2 hours.
Trap: "Loosen it every so often." Leave it on; responders and the hospital decide removal.
Trap: "Any tourniquet on the internet is fine." Look-alike tourniquets are sold online. ACS teaching ties tourniquet safety to recommended models, so buy a recommended model from a reputable medical supplier.
Trap: "Practice with your real tourniquet." Keep a separate trainer. ACS warns that repeatedly used training tourniquets can fail.

• Practice self-application on each arm with your trainer, one-handed, against a timer.
  • Know where your kit lives: car, bag, home.
  • Take an in-person Stop the Bleed course; the hands-on packing and tourniquet practice is the point of it.

cards.q: What does ACS say about improvised tourniquets?
cards.a: They are much less effective than commercial ones and hard to make and apply well.

cards.q: Why does a partly tightened tourniquet make bleeding worse?
cards.a: It blocks venous return while arterial flow continues.

cards.q: No tourniquet available for a limb bleed. What do you do?
cards.a: Hard direct pressure, then wound packing with pressure on top.

cards.q: Should a bystander ever loosen a tourniquet to restore circulation?
cards.a: No. Leave it on and tell responders the time it went on.

concepts.n: Junctional wounds and bleeding control kits
concepts.s: Wounds in the neck, armpit, or groin cannot take a limb tourniquet and need packing with hard pressure, and a public-access bleeding control kit holds the tools for both.

x.b:
• Junctional areas are where a limb meets the torso (armpit, groin) plus the neck. A limb tourniquet has no place to go above the wound there.
  • ACS teaching: pack the wound and hold firm pressure. A University of Texas Stop the Bleed flyer gives the same order: open the clothing, find the most active bleeding, and pack firmly onto the bleeding site with hemostatic gauze, a gauze roll, or clean cloth.
  • Torso wounds cannot be packed or tourniqueted effectively by bystanders; apply pressure and get the person to a trauma center as fast as possible.

Binghamton University's individual Stop the Bleed kits, a typical public-access configuration, contain:

  • A windlass tourniquet (C-A-T) and a SWAT-T elastic tourniquet.
  • Hemostatic gauze (Celox, 3 inches by 5 feet).
  • Two pairs of nitrile gloves.
  • A marker (for writing the tourniquet time).
  • Trauma shears (for exposing wounds).
  • Instruction sheet.

The 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines say it is reasonable to leave an open chest wound exposed to air, or cover it with a clean, dry, nonocclusive dressing such as gauze, or a vented chest seal.

Trap: Taping a sealed plastic square over a chest wound. Non-vented occlusion can trap air in the chest; the guideline options are exposed, nonocclusive, or vented.

• Where is the nearest public bleeding control kit at work, at the gym, and in your car?
  • Is your kit tourniquet a recommended commercial model, and is the trainer kept separate?
  • Can you reach and apply your tourniquet with either hand?

cards.q: Which body areas count as junctional for bleeding control?
cards.a: The armpit, groin, and (in Stop the Bleed teaching) the neck.

cards.q: How do you control a bleeding groin wound?
cards.a: Pack it firmly onto the bleeding source and hold hard pressure.

cards.q: What is the marker in a bleeding control kit for?
cards.a: Writing the time the tourniquet was applied.

cards.q: What dressing options do the 2024 guidelines give for an open chest wound?
cards.a: Leave it exposed, cover with a clean dry nonocclusive dressing, or use a vented chest seal.

concepts.s: For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally, call 911, get an AED, and push hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100 to 120 per minute and at least 2 inches deep.

x.b:
• Rate: 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
  • Depth: at least 2 inches (5 cm) for an average adult. The adult BLS guideline also says to avoid going deeper than 2.4 inches (6 cm).
  • Recoil: let the chest come fully back up; do not lean on it between compressions.
  • Hands: two hands on the lower half of the breastbone.
  • Ratio if giving breaths: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
  • Pauses: keep interruptions under 10 seconds.

1. Check responsiveness and breathing (no breathing or only gasping means arrest).
  2. Call 911 on speaker and send someone for an AED.
  3. Start compressions on a firm surface. The 2025 guidelines suggest the chest should be roughly at the level of the rescuer's knees.
  4. Use the AED as soon as it arrives; resume compressions immediately after each shock or no-shock message.
  5. Swap compressors about every 2 minutes if help is available; fatigue drops quality quickly.

The 2025 AHA adult BLS guideline says a compression-only approach is appropriate when lay rescuers are untrained or unwilling to give breaths, and it encourages trained rescuers to add breaths. Dispatchers are told to coach Hands-Only CPR for adults and CPR with breaths for children.

Synthesis: For an adult who suddenly collapses, compressions are the part that matters most and should never wait on breaths. Breaths matter more for children, drowning, and overdose, where the arrest starts with a breathing problem.

• A single, unified Chain of Survival for all cardiac arrests: prevention and preparedness, recognition and activation, high-quality CPR, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-arrest care, and recovery.
  • Lay rescuers should not use cognitive aids during a resuscitation (AHA 2025 highlights).
  • CPR training should begin in children younger than 12.

Trap: Stopping because a rib cracks. Rib fractures are a known consequence of effective compressions; keep going.
Trap: Compressing too shallow and too slow, which is the common real-world failure. Push at least 2 inches at 100 to 120 per minute; the beat of a song at that tempo helps.

cards.q: Adult compression rate per 2025 AHA guidelines?
cards.a: 100 to 120 per minute.

cards.q: Adult compression depth?
cards.a: At least 2 inches (5 cm), avoiding more than 2.4 inches (6 cm).

cards.q: Compression to breath ratio for a lay rescuer giving breaths?
cards.a: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

cards.q: When is Hands-Only CPR appropriate for an adult?
cards.a: When the rescuer is untrained or unwilling to give breaths; dispatchers coach it for adults.

cards.q: Maximum pause in compressions?
cards.a: Under 10 seconds.

concepts.s: Children and infants get CPR with breaths at the same 100 to 120 per minute rate, compressed at least one third of chest depth, and the 2025 AHA guidelines dropped the two-finger infant technique.

x.b:
• Infant: under 1 year (newborns are a separate protocol).
  • Child: 1 year to puberty.
  • Adult: puberty and older.

• Rate: 100 to 120 per minute for all ages.
  • Child depth: about 2 inches, at least one third of chest depth. One or two hands on the lower half of the breastbone depending on size.
  • Infant depth: about 1.5 inches, at least one third of chest depth, at the center of the chest just below the nipple line.
  • Ratio for a single lay rescuer: 30:2.
  • Alone with no phone: give about 2 minutes (5 cycles of 30:2) of CPR before leaving to call 911 and get an AED.

The 2025 AHA and American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines recommend the heel of one hand or the two-thumb encircling-hands technique for infants. If you cannot encircle the chest, use the heel of one hand. The long-used two-finger technique is no longer recommended because it often failed to reach adequate depth.

The 2025 guidelines direct dispatchers to coach conventional CPR with breaths for children. Pediatric arrest more often starts with a breathing problem, so oxygen delivery matters more than in sudden adult collapse.

Trap: Learning infant CPR from an older course or video that shows two fingers. That technique was removed in 2025.

cards.q: Infant compression depth?
cards.a: About 1.5 inches, at least one third of chest depth.

cards.q: Child compression depth?
cards.a: About 2 inches, at least one third of chest depth.

cards.q: Which infant compression technique did the 2025 AHA guidelines drop?
cards.a: The two-finger technique; use the heel of one hand or two thumbs with encircling hands.

cards.q: Alone with no phone and an unresponsive child, what first?
cards.a: About 2 minutes (5 cycles) of CPR, then go call 911 and get an AED.

cards.q: Do dispatchers coach Hands-Only or conventional CPR for children?
cards.a: Conventional CPR with breaths.

concepts.s: Turn the AED on and follow its voice prompts, place pads on bare skin, keep everyone clear during analysis and shock, and restart compressions immediately afterward.

x.b:
1. Turn the AED on and follow the prompts.
  2. Expose and dry the chest.
  3. Place one pad on the upper right chest and the other on the lower left side, a few inches below the left armpit.
  4. If pads might touch (small person), place one in the center of the chest and one on the back.
  5. Make sure no one is touching the person and say "CLEAR" before analysis and before a shock.
  6. After a shock, or if no shock is advised, start CPR immediately with compressions.

• The AED decides whether to shock. You cannot shock someone who does not need it with a standard public AED.
  • The 2025 AHA guidelines say it may be reasonable to move a bra rather than remove it when placing pads.
  • Red Cross adult steps cover children 8 and older or over 55 pounds. For younger children, AHA teaching uses pediatric pads or a pediatric setting if the device has one, and adult pads otherwise.
  • The 2025 AHA guidelines emphasize public-access defibrillation as a pillar of the Chain of Survival.

Trap: Waiting to start CPR until the AED arrives. CPR continues until the AED is applied, and resumes right after each analysis.
Trap: Pausing for a long pulse or breathing check after a shock. Go straight back to compressions; the AED will reanalyze on its own schedule.
Trap: Being afraid of hurting the person. A person in cardiac arrest is clinically dead; the AED only shocks a shockable rhythm.

cards.q: Standard adult AED pad positions?
cards.a: Upper right chest and lower left side a few inches below the armpit.

cards.q: What do you do immediately after the AED delivers a shock?
cards.a: Restart CPR, beginning with compressions.

cards.q: What if adult-sized pads would touch on a small child?
cards.a: Place one on the center of the chest and one on the back.

cards.q: Can a public AED shock someone who does not need it?
cards.a: No. It analyzes the rhythm and only advises a shock for a shockable rhythm.

concepts.s: For severe choking, the 2025 AHA guidelines recommend cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts for adults and children, and 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts for infants, with CPR if the person becomes unresponsive.

x.b: Mild obstruction: the person can cough forcefully, speak, or cry; encourage coughing and watch. Severe obstruction: cannot speak, cough, cry, or breathe effectively. The Red Cross code card says to keep working until the person can cough forcefully, speak, cry, or breathe.

1. Call 911 (or have someone call).
  2. Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand.
  3. Give 5 abdominal thrusts (stand behind, fist just above the navel, quick inward and upward thrusts).
  4. Repeat cycles until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive.

For a person in late pregnancy, or when you cannot reach around the abdomen, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. AHA lay courses had long taught abdominal thrusts on their own for adults; the 2025 guidelines add back blows to the sequence.

1. Support the infant face down along your forearm, head lower than the chest, holding the jaw.
  2. Give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades.
  3. Turn face up, supporting the head, and give 5 chest thrusts on the center of the breastbone.
  4. Repeat until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive.

The 2025 guidelines state abdominal thrusts are not recommended for infants.

Red Cross code card for all ages:

  • Lower them to a firm, flat surface and start CPR with 30 compressions.
  • Before giving breaths, open the mouth and look. Remove an object only if you can see it. No blind finger sweeps.
  • Attempt 2 breaths and continue cycles, checking the mouth before each set of breaths. Use an AED as soon as one is available.

Trap: Blind finger sweeps. They can push the object deeper; remove only what you can see.
Trap: Abdominal thrusts on an infant. Use chest thrusts.
Trap: Slapping the back of someone who is coughing forcefully. A strong cough is the best clearance mechanism; intervene when coughing becomes ineffective.

cards.q: 2025 AHA sequence for a responsive choking adult?
cards.a: Repeated cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts.

cards.q: Choking infant sequence?
cards.a: Repeated cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; no abdominal thrusts.

cards.q: Choking pregnant woman or someone you cannot reach around?
cards.a: Use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.

cards.q: Choking person becomes unresponsive. What next?
cards.a: Lower them to the ground, call 911 if not done, and start CPR, looking in the mouth before breaths.

cards.q: When may you sweep the mouth?
cards.a: Only if you can see the object; never blind sweeps.

concepts.s: Chest pain or discomfort with spread to the arm, jaw, neck, or back, shortness of breath, nausea, or lightheadedness means call 911 at once, and women more often have symptoms other than chest pain.

x.b:
The AHA Mission: Lifeline poster lists:

  • Pain or discomfort in the chest.
  • Lightheadedness, nausea, or vomiting.
  • Jaw, neck, or back pain.
  • Discomfort or pain in the arm or shoulder.
  • Shortness of breath.

AHA's Go Red for Women material adds that women are more likely to have symptoms other than chest pain, such as upper abdominal pressure, indigestion, fainting, or extreme fatigue.

1. Call 911 immediately. The 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines say to activate EMS for transport to the closest emergency department.
  2. Do not drive yourself (AHA).
  3. Keep the person resting and calm.
  4. Aspirin: the 2024 guidelines say an alert adult with nontraumatic chest pain may be encouraged to chew and swallow aspirin unless they have a known aspirin allergy or a clinician has told them not to take it. If there is any doubt, the guideline says it is reasonable to wait for EMS without giving it.
  5. If they collapse and stop breathing normally, start CPR and get an AED.

A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to heart muscle; the person is usually awake and talking. Cardiac arrest is the heart stopping effectively; the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. A heart attack can trigger cardiac arrest.

Trap: Waiting to see if it passes, or calling it indigestion. Women in particular are more likely to dismiss atypical symptoms, per AHA material.
Trap: Giving aspirin to someone with a known allergy or who has been told to avoid it, or to someone with trauma-related chest pain. The guideline limits it to alert adults with nontraumatic chest pain.

cards.q: List four heart attack warning signs from the AHA.
cards.a: Chest pain or discomfort, arm or shoulder discomfort, jaw/neck/back pain, shortness of breath (also lightheadedness, nausea).

cards.q: Should someone with heart attack symptoms drive to the ER?
cards.a: No. Call 911.

cards.q: Who may be encouraged to chew aspirin under the 2024 guidelines?
cards.a: An alert adult with nontraumatic chest pain and no known allergy or medical advice against it.

cards.q: Heart attack versus cardiac arrest in one line?
cards.a: Heart attack is a blocked artery in an awake person; cardiac arrest is an unresponsive person not breathing normally.

concepts.s: Use the FAST check (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911) to spot a stroke, call 911 immediately, and note when symptoms started.

x.b:
• Face drooping: ask them to smile. Is one side uneven?
  • Arm weakness: ask them to raise both arms. Does one drift down?
  • Speech difficulty: slurred or strange speech, or cannot repeat a simple sentence.
  • Time to call 911.

• The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines say to activate EMS immediately for suspected stroke and to use a recognition scale such as FAST.
  • Measuring blood glucose is reasonable if a meter is available and it does not delay EMS.
  • FAST is not validated in children. If pediatric stroke is suspected, call EMS; adult stroke scales should not be the only tool.

Some hospitals teach BE-FAST, adding Balance and Eyes (vision loss) to catch strokes in the back of the brain that FAST can miss. The AHA, the American Stroke Association, and the 2024 first aid guideline use FAST.

Synthesis: Learn FAST as the core test and treat sudden loss of balance or vision as stroke warning signs too. Neither tool rules out stroke; a normal check with a strong suspicion still means call 911.

Note the time the person was last known to be normal, and tell EMS. Treatment options depend on it.

Trap: Letting the person "sleep it off" or waiting to see if symptoms clear. Symptoms that resolve can be a transient ischemic attack, which still needs emergency evaluation.

cards.q: What does F.A.S.T. stand for?
cards.a: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911.

cards.q: What do the B and E in BE-FAST add?
cards.a: Balance and Eyes (vision), to catch strokes FAST can miss.

cards.q: What time should you report to EMS for a suspected stroke?
cards.a: When the person was last known to be normal.

cards.q: Is FAST validated for children?
cards.a: No; call EMS for suspected pediatric stroke and do not rely on adult scales alone.

concepts.s: Protect a seizing person from injury, never restrain them or put anything in their mouth, time the seizure, roll them on their side, and call 911 for a seizure over 5 minutes or any red-flag situation.

x.b:
1. Stay with the person and stay calm. Move nearby hard or sharp objects.
  2. If they are falling, ease them to the ground.
  3. Roll them onto one side to keep the airway clear. Put something soft and flat under the head.
  4. Remove eyeglasses and loosen anything tight around the neck.
  5. Time the seizure.
  6. Afterward, help them sit somewhere safe and reassure them as they become alert.

• Do not hold them down or try to stop their movements.
  • Do not put anything in their mouth. The 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines list this as harmful.
  • Do not give mouth-to-mouth during the seizure.
  • Do not give food, water, or pills until they are fully alert.

The 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines and CDC lists overlap:

  • First-ever seizure.
  • Seizure lasting more than 5 minutes.
  • Repeated seizures without returning to normal between them.
  • Seizure in water, with injury, or with trouble breathing or choking.
  • Seizure in an infant under 6 months or in pregnancy.
  • Not back to baseline mental status within 5 to 10 minutes after the seizure stops (AHA/Red Cross).
  • Has diabetes and lost consciousness (CDC).

Trap: "They'll swallow their tongue." They cannot; objects in the mouth cause broken teeth, bites, and choking.
Trap: Calling 911 for every known epileptic's typical brief seizure. If it matches their usual pattern, ends within 5 minutes, and they recover, they may not need EMS; check for a medical ID or seizure plan.

cards.q: Seizure duration that warrants 911?
cards.a: More than 5 minutes.

cards.q: Two things you must never do during a seizure?
cards.a: Restrain the person or put anything in their mouth.

cards.q: How should you position someone during a generalized seizure?
cards.a: On their side, with something soft under the head and the area cleared.

cards.q: Name three other reasons to call 911 for a seizure.
cards.a: First seizure, seizure in water or with injury, repeated seizures, breathing trouble, pregnancy, infant under 6 months.

concepts.s: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction treated with epinephrine as early as possible, and a first aider should help the person use their own auto-injector in the outer thigh and call 911.

x.b: Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction. Red Cross material describes airway swelling that makes breathing hard. Other common signs include hives or flushing, swelling of lips, tongue, or throat, wheezing, vomiting, and faintness or collapse.

• 2024 AHA/Red Cross: if an epinephrine auto-injector is available, the person should self-administer it, and a first aid provider should help if needed. Activate EMS.
  • Early intramuscular epinephrine in the outer thigh is the primary treatment, per the guideline's supporting text.
  • A repeat dose may be considered if there is no response to the first and EMS will take more than 5 to 10 minutes to arrive (2024 guideline).

1. Remove the safety cap.
  2. Press the tip firmly against the middle of the outer thigh until it clicks. It works through clothing (KidsHealth/Nemours).
  3. Hold it in place for the time on the device label. Hold times differ by brand: KidsHealth gives 3 seconds for EpiPen, 2 seconds for Auvi-Q, and up to 10 seconds for some generics; Canadian Red Cross material says 10 seconds.
  4. Call 911 (or have someone call while you inject).
  5. Have the person lie down if they can; sitting if breathing is easier.
  6. Give a second dose if symptoms do not improve, get worse, or return, following the device instructions.

The FDA approved neffy, the first epinephrine nasal spray, on August 9, 2024, for people weighing at least 30 kg (about 66 lb). The label allows a second dose in the same nostril with a new device if symptoms do not improve or worsen.

Trap: Giving an antihistamine and waiting. Epinephrine is first-line; antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
Trap: Skipping 911 because the person feels better after the injection. Symptoms can return; they still need emergency care.
Trap: Fumbling with an unfamiliar device. Read the label diagram; brands differ in which end goes on the thigh and how long to hold.

cards.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector given?
cards.a: The middle of the outer thigh, through clothing if needed.

cards.q: How long do you hold an auto-injector in place?
cards.a: As the label says; it varies by brand (about 2 to 10 seconds).

cards.q: When do the 2024 guidelines say a repeat epinephrine dose may be considered?
cards.a: No response to the first dose and EMS more than 5 to 10 minutes away.

cards.q: After using an auto-injector and the person improves, do you still call 911?
cards.a: Yes. Symptoms can return.

cards.q: What is neffy?
cards.a: An FDA-approved epinephrine nasal spray (2024) for people at least 30 kg.

concepts.s: For a suspected opioid overdose, call 911, give naloxone as soon as you can, support breathing or start CPR if the person is not breathing normally, and stay with them.

x.b:
• Small, constricted "pinpoint" pupils.
  • Falling asleep or loss of consciousness; limp body.
  • Slow, shallow breathing.
  • Choking or gurgling sounds.
  • EMS1's summary of the 2025 AHA guidelines also lists blue or gray skin.

1. Try to wake them: shout and rub the breastbone.
  2. Call 911.
  3. Give naloxone right away. CDC: do not wait for emergency workers to arrive before giving it.
  4. Unresponsive and not breathing normally: the 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines say to give high-quality CPR (compressions plus breaths) and naloxone. The 2025 AHA guidelines add that naloxone should not interfere with CPR.
  5. If breathing, place them on their side (CDC) and stay until help arrives.

• Narcan 4 mg nasal spray became available over the counter after FDA approval in March 2023.
  • One device is one dose. Lay the person on their back, insert the nozzle in one nostril, and press the plunger.
  • Product instructions: if there is no response after 2 to 3 minutes, give another dose in the other nostril with a new device, and repeat as needed.
  • CDC notes more than one dose may be needed, especially with illicitly manufactured fentanyl.

An opioid overdose kills by stopping breathing. That is why the AHA/Red Cross recommendation for overdose specifies compressions plus ventilation, unlike Hands-Only CPR for sudden adult collapse.

Trap: Leaving once the person wakes up. Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, so breathing can stop again. Stay with them.
Trap: Assuming naloxone is dangerous if it turns out not to be an opioid overdose. It acts only on opioid receptors, which is why it is sold over the counter and the guidelines encourage giving it on suspicion.

cards.q: Classic signs of opioid overdose?
cards.a: Pinpoint pupils, unresponsiveness, slow or absent breathing, gurgling, blue or gray skin.

cards.q: Should you wait for EMS before giving naloxone?
cards.a: No. CDC says give it as soon as possible.

cards.q: No response 2 to 3 minutes after nasal naloxone. What next?
cards.a: Give another dose in the other nostril with a new device.

cards.q: Overdose victim unresponsive and not breathing normally: Hands-Only or full CPR?
cards.a: CPR with compressions plus breaths, and naloxone, per the 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines.

cards.q: Why stay with someone after naloxone revives them?
cards.a: It can wear off before the opioid, so breathing may stop again.

concepts.s: For a suspected poisoning in a person who is awake and breathing, call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222, and call 911 if they collapse, seize, or have trouble breathing.

x.b:
• Poison Help line: 1-800-222-1222 (HRSA). It routes to your local poison center. Use it for swallowed medicines or chemicals, exposures, and "is this dangerous?" questions.
  • 911 if the person is unresponsive, not breathing normally, having a seizure, or having trouble breathing.
  • Have the container in hand when you call: product name, amount, time, and the person's age and weight.

x.t: Chemical on the skin (2024 AHA/Red Cross)
x.b:
• Decontaminate immediately.
  • Irrigate skin exposed to a caustic chemical with running water for at least 15 minutes.
  • Remove contaminated clothing and jewelry.
  • Following local guidance or consulting a regional poison center for chemical-specific steps can be beneficial.
  • Call EMS for respiratory or systemic symptoms.

Trap: Making the person vomit or using syrup of ipecac. Poison centers and pediatric guidance abandoned this years ago; vomiting can cause more injury, especially with caustics. Call Poison Help instead.
Trap: Waiting for symptoms before calling. Many poisonings (acetaminophen is a classic example) look fine early. Call when exposure happens.
Trap: Brushing off a chemical before flushing without protecting yourself. Wear gloves and avoid contaminating yourself.

cards.q: US Poison Help phone number?
When should a poisoning go to 911 instead of Poison Help?
cards.a: Unresponsive, not breathing normally, seizing, or trouble breathing.

cards.q: How long should skin exposed to a caustic chemical be flushed?
cards.a: With running water for at least 15 minutes (2024 AHA/Red Cross).

cards.q: Should you induce vomiting after a poisoning?
cards.a: No. Call Poison Help for instructions.

concepts.s: Shock is life-threatening circulatory failure that shows as pale or gray skin, a fast pulse, fast breathing, and confusion, and first aid is to call 911, treat the cause, lay the person down, and keep them warm.

x.b:
• Pale or ashen skin; blue or gray lips or fingernails.
  • Rapid pulse; rapid, shallow breathing.
  • Nausea or vomiting; enlarged pupils.
  • Weakness, dizziness, or fainting.
  • Anxiety, restlessness, or confusion; loss of consciousness.

1. Call 911.
  2. Fix the cause you can: control bleeding (Stop the Bleed), give epinephrine for anaphylaxis.
  3. Have the person lie down. Mayo advises raising the legs slightly unless that causes pain, injury, or breathing trouble.
  4. Keep them warm with a blanket or clothing.
  5. Give nothing to eat or drink.
  6. Start CPR if there are no signs of life.

Synthesis: Shock is the body losing the ability to deliver blood to organs, from blood loss, severe allergy, infection, or heart failure. First aid cannot reverse most causes, so the job is to stop what you can stop (bleeding above all), reduce heat loss, and shorten the time to hospital care.

Trap: Giving water to a shocky trauma patient who says they are thirsty. They may need surgery and can vomit; give nothing by mouth.
Trap: Raising the legs of someone with a suspected spine, hip, or leg injury. Leave them flat.
Trap: Thinking a calm, talkative patient is fine. Early shock often shows as anxiety and a fast pulse before blood pressure falls.

cards.q: Name four signs of shock.
cards.a: Pale or gray skin, rapid pulse, rapid shallow breathing, confusion or anxiety (also weakness, nausea).

cards.q: How should a person in shock be positioned?
cards.a: Lying down, legs slightly raised unless it causes pain, injury, or breathing trouble.

cards.q: Food or drink for someone in shock?
cards.a: None.

cards.q: Why keep a shock patient warm?
cards.a: Heat loss worsens shock and bleeding; cover them with a blanket or clothing.

concepts.s: Cool a burn under cool running water as soon as possible for at least 10 and ideally 20 minutes, never with ice or butter, then cover it loosely and get care for large, deep, or high-risk burns.

x.b:
• Red Cross Scientific Advisory Council: cool or cold running potable water for a minimum of 10 minutes, ideally 20. Avoid cooling beyond 40 minutes because of hypothermia risk.
  • NHS: 20 minutes under cool running water, as soon as possible and within 3 hours. The Red Cross advisory also says cooling may help up to 3 hours after injury.
  • No running water: a clean cool or cold compress that is not frozen (Red Cross) or cool bottled water or a wet towel (NHS).
  • Watch for hypothermia when cooling large burns or small children (Red Cross).

The sources differ slightly on minimum duration (10 versus 20 minutes); both say 20 is the goal.

• Remove clothing and jewelry near the burn, but leave anything stuck to it.
  • Cover with cling film laid over the burn, not wrapped around a limb, or a clean nonfluffy dressing.
  • Do not burst blisters or use adhesive plasters.
  • Paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen can help with pain.

• Large or deep burns.
  • Burns on the face, genitals, or bottom.
  • Chemical or electrical burns.
  • Any burn in a young child (NHS asks parents to call 111 for any child under 5).

Chemical burns get prolonged flushing with water (see Poisoning and chemical exposure). Electrical burns can hide internal damage, so scene safety (power off) comes first.

Trap: Butter, oil, creams, toothpaste, or other home remedies. NHS says no creams, oils, or butter; they trap heat and complicate assessment.
Trap: Ice or ice water. The Red Cross advisory says do not use ice, including ice packs, because it can deepen the injury.
Trap: Stopping cooling after a minute because the pain eased. Keep going for the full time.

cards.q: How long should you cool a thermal burn?
cards.a: At least 10 and ideally 20 minutes under cool running water (Red Cross); NHS says 20 minutes.

cards.q: Up to how long after a burn does cooling still help?
cards.a: Up to 3 hours, per both NHS and the Red Cross advisory.

cards.q: Why no ice on a burn?
cards.a: It can worsen the tissue injury (Red Cross advisory).

cards.q: How should cling film be applied to a burn?
cards.a: Laid over it, not wrapped around the limb.

cards.q: Name three burns that need emergency care.
cards.a: Large or deep burns; burns on the face, genitals, or buttocks; chemical or electrical burns.

concepts.s: Immobilize a suspected fracture in the position found, control bleeding from open fractures, treat sprains with rest, cold, compression, and elevation, and leave a suspected spine injury still if the person is breathing normally.

x.b:
• Signs: deformity, severe pain, swelling, inability to use the limb, or bone through the skin.
  • Support the injured part in the position you find it. Do not try to straighten it.
  • For an open fracture, control bleeding with pressure around the bone end (do not push the bone back in) and cover with a clean dressing.
  • Call 911 for open fractures, large-bone injuries (thigh, pelvis), deformed limbs with numbness or a cold, pale hand or foot, or any suspected neck or back injury.

A Royal Berkshire NHS leaflet gives:

  • Rest the injury.
  • Ice wrapped in a cloth (or frozen peas in a towel) for 10 to 20 minutes at a time, at least 30 minutes apart, for the first 24 to 48 hours. Never directly on skin.
  • Compression with a stretchy bandage, not tight, removed at night.
  • Elevation above heart level when possible.

Persistent pain or inability to use the area beyond 2 to 3 days can mean a missed hairline fracture.

The 2024 AHA/Red Cross guidelines: if the injury suggests a neck, back, hip, or pelvic injury and the person is responsive and breathing normally, leave them in the position found unless the area is unsafe. If they need CPR, CPR takes priority and they go on their back.

Trap: Straightening a deformed limb to splint it. Splint as found and let EMS manage alignment.
Trap: Applying ice directly to the skin. Wrap it.
Trap: Moving a possible spine injury "to be safe." Only move them if the scene is dangerous or they need CPR.

cards.q: How should a suspected fracture be immobilized?
cards.a: In the position found, without straightening it.

cards.q: What does RICE stand for?
cards.a: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.

cards.q: Ice timing for a sprain per the NHS leaflet?
cards.a: 10 to 20 minutes at a time, at least 30 minutes apart, for the first 24 to 48 hours, wrapped.

cards.q: Suspected spine injury, responsive, breathing normally. Move them?
cards.a: No; leave them as found unless the area is unsafe or CPR is needed.

concepts.s: After a blow to the head, watch for CDC danger signs such as a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, unequal pupils, seizures, or growing confusion, which require emergency care.

x.b: Confusion, nausea, balance problems, blurry vision, sensitivity to light and noise, and dizziness. Loss of consciousness is not required for a concussion.

x.t: Danger signs: go to the ED or call 911 (CDC)
x.b:
• Headache that gets worse and does not go away.
  • Weakness, numbness, or decreased coordination.
  • Repeated vomiting or nausea.
  • Slurred speech.
  • Unusual drowsiness or cannot be woken.
  • One pupil larger than the other.
  • Convulsions or seizures.
  • Cannot recognize people or places; increasing confusion, restlessness, or agitation; unusual behavior.

• If they are unresponsive, check breathing and start CPR if needed.
  • If the mechanism suggests a neck injury and the person is breathing normally, keep them still (2024 AHA/Red Cross positioning guidance).
  • Control scalp bleeding with direct pressure; scalp wounds bleed heavily.
  • Someone with a suspected concussion should stop the activity and be evaluated before returning to sport.

Trap: "They were never knocked out, so it's not a concussion." Most concussions happen without loss of consciousness.
Trap: Treating a lucid interval as recovery. A person who seems fine and then becomes drowsy or confused is showing a danger sign.
Trap: Leaving someone with a recent head injury alone. Have someone stay and watch for danger signs.

cards.q: Name four CDC concussion danger signs.
cards.a: Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, unequal pupils, seizures (also slurred speech, cannot be woken, growing confusion).

cards.q: Is loss of consciousness required for a concussion?
cards.a: No.

cards.q: Head injury victim seems fine, then grows drowsy and confused. What does that mean?
cards.a: A danger sign; get emergency care.

cards.q: What should a player with a suspected concussion do?
cards.a: Stop playing and get evaluated before returning.

concepts.s: For a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 to 15 minutes, and seek emergency care if it lasts beyond 15 minutes or follows a serious injury.

x.b:
1. Sit down and lean forward, breathing through the mouth so blood drains out instead of down the throat.
  2. Pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils for at least 10 to 15 minutes without letting go to check.
  3. A cold pack wrapped in a towel on the bridge of the nose can help, but keep pinching.
  4. Stay upright; do not lie down.

• Bleeding longer than 15 minutes: go to an emergency department or call emergency services.
  • Heavy bleeding with a lot of blood lost, difficulty breathing, or vomiting after swallowing a lot of blood.
  • Nosebleed after a serious injury such as a car crash.
  • People on blood thinners or with clotting disorders should get advice if it does not stop.

Trap: Tilting the head back. Blood runs down the throat, which hides how much is being lost and can cause vomiting or choking. Lean forward.
Trap: Pinching the bony bridge. Pressure must be on the soft part, below the bone, where the bleeding vessels are.
Trap: Releasing every minute to check. Hold continuously for the full time.

cards.q: Head position for a nosebleed?
cards.a: Sit up and lean forward.

cards.q: Where and how long do you pinch?
cards.a: The soft part just above the nostrils, for at least 10 to 15 minutes.

cards.q: Why not tilt the head back?
cards.a: Blood runs down the throat, which can cause vomiting or choking and hides the bleeding.

cards.q: Nosebleed duration that needs emergency care?
cards.a: Longer than 15 minutes.

concepts.s: Heat stroke is an emergency that needs immediate whole-body cooling, ideally cold-water immersion, while hypothermia needs gentle protection from further heat loss and rewarming without rubbing the limbs.

x.b:
• Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating; pale, cool, damp skin; fast weak pulse; nausea or vomiting; cramps; weakness; dizziness; headache; fainting. Move to a cool place, loosen clothes, cool wet cloths, sip water. Get help if vomiting, worsening, or lasting more than 1 hour.
  • Heat stroke: body temperature 103 F or higher; hot, red, dry or damp skin; fast strong pulse; headache, confusion, or passing out. Call 911, move to a cooler place, cool them down, and give nothing to drink.

• Heat stroke is heat illness with altered mental status: activate EMS.
  • For adults and children, it is reasonable to start immediate active cooling by whole-body (neck-down) immersion in cool to cold water, for 15 minutes or until neurological symptoms resolve (adult recommendation).
  • If immersion is not possible, use other active cooling: commercial ice packs, cold showers, and similar methods.
  • For trained rescuers measuring core temperature, the target to cool to is 39 C (102.2 F).
Synthesis: Cool first and fast. Time spent above dangerous core temperatures drives the damage, so immersion on scene beats waiting for transport when it is available.

• CDC warning signs in adults: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness. Infants: bright red, cold skin and very low energy.
  • Protect from further heat loss: get out of wind and wet and insulate from the ground. The guidelines say active rewarming through damp clothing with the hypothermia wrap technique is reasonable.
  • Decreased responsiveness: call EMS while rewarming by any available method.
  • Alert people who can swallow safely may have food or fluids.
  • Do not apply heat sources, rubbing, or massage to the arms and legs. Warm showers or warm-water immersion are potentially harmful. Small glove or boot chemical heat packs are not effective, and body-to-body rewarming offers no benefit over other active methods.

• Rewarm in clean lukewarm water at 37 to 40 C (about 99 to 104 F) at the earliest opportunity, only if there is no risk of refreezing.
  • Treat moderate to severe hypothermia (core rewarming) before frostbite.
  • Remove rings and constricting items; avoid walking on frozen feet; apply bulky, clean, dry dressings.
  • Do not break blisters; seek prompt medical care.

Trap: Giving fluids to someone with heat stroke. CDC says nothing to drink; altered mental status raises choking risk.
Trap: Rubbing frostbitten or cold limbs, or plunging a hypothermic person into a hot shower. Both are on the guidelines' do-not list.
Trap: Thawing frostbite when it could refreeze. Refreezing causes more damage than staying frozen until you reach shelter.

cards.q: What separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
cards.a: Altered mental status (confusion, collapse) and a very high body temperature, 103 F or higher per CDC.

cards.q: Preferred cooling for an adult with heat stroke?
cards.a: Whole-body (neck-down) cool to cold water immersion for 15 minutes or until neurological symptoms resolve.

cards.q: Core temperature target when cooling heat stroke?
Three things not to do to a hypothermic person?
cards.a: Rub or massage the limbs, apply heat to the extremities, or put them in a warm shower or bath.

cards.q: Water temperature for rewarming frostbite?
cards.a: Clean lukewarm water at 37 to 40 C, only if it will not refreeze.
